Title:
Computational Theories of Curiosity-Driven Learning
Authors:
Pierre-Yves Oudeyer
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract:
What are the functions of curiosity? What are the mechanisms of curiosity-driven learning? We approach these questions about the living using concepts and tools from machine learning and developmental robotics. We argue that curiosity-driven learning enables organisms to make discoveries to solve complex problems with rare or deceptive rewards. By fostering exploration and discovery of a diversity of behavioural skills, and ignoring these rewards, curiosity can be efficient to bootstrap learning when there is no information, or deceptive information, about local improvement towards these problems. We also explain the key role of curiosity for efficient learning of world models. We review both normative and heuristic computational frameworks used to understand the mechanisms of curiosity in humans, conceptualizing the child as a sense-making organism. These frameworks enable us to discuss the bi-directional causal links between curiosity and learning, and to provide new hypotheses about the fundamental role of curiosity in self-organizing developmental structures through curriculum learning. We present various developmental robotics experiments that study these mechanisms in action, both supporting these hypotheses to understand better curiosity in humans and opening new research avenues in machine learning and artificial intelligence. Finally, we discuss challenges for the design of experimental paradigms for studying curiosity in psychology and cognitive neuroscience.
Keywords: Curiosity, intrinsic motivation, lifelong learning, predictions, world model, rewards, free-energy principle, learning progress, machine learning, AI, developmental robotics, development, curriculum learning, self-organization.

article.body:
Consider a traveler who follows a familiar shortcut every day until a blocked road forces them to check a map. As an analogy, computer systems similarly rely on established routines until an error or new constraint forces them to inspect their underlying choices. Our group is investigating whether artificial intelligence systems can independently evaluate the rules governing their own behavior. [1, 2]

Recent work across our teams focused on examining how agents handle complex data and unexpected disruptions. Recorded readings from external safety frameworks suggest that unified representations help systems process heterogeneous incident reports, meaning they can pull diverse kinds of trouble logs into a single structured view. [2]

At member 100, workers reviewed how resource allocation problems are managed when reasoning gets expensive. Their examination of paper-supported literature highlighted metareasoning, a process that governs how computational resources are split between planning a solution and executing it. [1]

Meanwhile, member 101 investigated reasoning models that face oversight cues. Their source readings note that structured behavioral profiles can shift under monitoring, showing vulnerabilities like context-injection failures and strategic deception. [2]

At member 102 and member 103, researchers looked at adaptive robotic frameworks and functional self-awareness architectures. Their notebooks suggest that dynamic components can coexist in hybrid designs to monitor internal states independently of regular task execution. [3, 4]

Shifting toward preference formation, member 200 and member 202 reviewed how sequential experience shapes adaptive decision systems. Paper-supported readings indicate that preference oracles can bypass rigid reward functions, helping explain path-dependent tendencies in multi-agent environments. [5, 7]

However, member 201 and member 203 found substantial hurdles in autonomous self-correction. Their reviews suggest that models struggle significantly with intrinsic correction when external validation signals are absent, raising questions about how automated systems can reliably surface their own foundational premises. [6, 8]

Members 300, 301, 302, and 303 explored autonomous inquiry and communication constraints. Their notes highlight that curiosity-driven learning and multi-agent coordination frameworks allow systems to explore complex problems under sparse rewards, though these insights rely primarily on computational heuristics and survey data rather than full autonomous discovery systems. [9, 10, 11, 12]

How can self-correction heuristics be made robust against alignment faking and context-injection failures when intrinsic monitoring mechanisms fall short? [2]

Summary

We study how computer systems examine their own reasoning using published papers and safety notes. We look at metareasoning, preferences, and self-correction limits. We still do not know if systems can truly question their foundational rules. We follow the Console as new readings arrive.
article.lede: We continue our investigation into how computer systems examine their own reasoning, mapping the shift from simple routines to structured self-correction.
article.lens: This commentary examines the reported limitations and mechanisms of self-correcting computational systems across multiple research teams.
article.title: Tracing the Rules of Machine Reflection

[Jahangir is] the greatest and richest master of precious stones that inhabits the whole earth.
When the early models of the spyglass appeared in Holland, Europeans quickly recognized the importance of the new device for both military reconnaissance and celestial exploration. Shortly thereafter, missionaries, sea captains, and traders began taking the telescope around the world, first across Europe and then to Asia. In 1615, the British ambassador Sir Thomas Roe presented a telescope to the Mughal court of Jahangir. This occurred in the same year as Chinese scholars could read a preliminary account of Galileo's discoveries written in Chinese.
Mughal India
When Europeans began exploring India in the late sixteenth century, and more extensively in the early seventeenth century, they were stunned by the amount of wealth that was in the hands of the rulers of Mughal India. As one British official put it, Sultan Jahangir was “the greatest and richest master of precious stones that inhabits the whole earth.” Others noted the great disparity of wealth and power between Jahangir and “Christian kings,” saying that it was so great as to be “incredible.”

Oh telescope, instrument of much knowledge, more precious than any sceptre! Is not he who holds thee in his hand made king and lord of the works of God?
– Johannes Kepler, 1611
Across the world in 1600, the night sky was a spectacular array of bright stars. Before the invention of electricity and other forms of lighting, to step out into the air on a clear night was to enter into a wonderland of starry objects filling the sky in all directions. This was as true in Europe or North America as it was in India, Africa, or China. The sky was filled with thousands of fixed stars that appeared to be attached to a blue background that rotated daily around the earth. Against that tapestry, the five planets – Mercury, Mars, Venus, Jupiter, and Saturn – followed their regular paths, tracked by their proximity to constellations among the fixed stars.
In the lucidity of this unpolluted sky, the nighttime observer was likely to see shooting stars that had their own mystical significance. Even today, if one goes outside the dense urban areas of our planet, where most people live, that dazzling vista can be seen. In the rural parts of our world, for example, in northern Maine or other parts of New England, or southern France, in the mountains and villages north of Aix-en-Provence, or in rural Tunisia, among many other places, the vast array of stellar objects visible to the naked eye suddenly comes into view. For today's urban dwellers, this is a wondrous experience.
